paper_metadata.title: Unsupervised Quantum Anomaly Detection on Noisy Quantum Processors

summary: The paper evaluates a projected quantum-kernel one-class SVM for fraud detection using a 10‑qubit feature map and partial state tomography. On a 20‑feature Sparkov credit‑card dataset (500 samples at anomaly ratio r=0.2), the quantum kernel models achieve mean F1 scores around ~0.83–0.85 compared to a classical rbf‑OCSVM baseline of 0.757, and the pipeline is experimentally executed on AQT Ibex, IonQ Harmony, and IBM Eagle/Falcon devices with ~200 tomography shots per sample.

experiments.description: Projected quantum-kernel one-class SVM anomaly detection on a subsampled Sparkov credit-card fraud dataset, evaluated in simulation across three hardware-efficient feature maps and compared against a classical rbf-OCSVM baseline.

algorithm.variant: One-Class Quantum Support Vector Machine with projected quantum radial basis function (qrbf) kernel
algorithm.optimizer: LIBSVM / quadratic programming solver (for OCSVM dual)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each 20-dimensional sample is encoded into a hardware-efficient quantum circuit using single-qubit RX and RZ rotations plus entangling gates; projected kernels are built from one-qubit reduced density matrices obtained by partial tomography.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Unsupervised anomaly detection via OCSVM dual objective min_(alpha) 1/2 alpha^T K alpha subject to 0 <= alpha_i <= 1 and e^T alpha = nu l, with K replaced by projected quantum kernel K_gamma(x_i,x_j)=exp(-gamma sum_k ||rho_k(x_i)-rho_k(x_j)||_F^2).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: OCSVM dual constraints; no QUBO/penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Financial fraud detection on a feature-engineered Sparkov credit-card transactions dataset, subsampled to vary anomaly ratio.
problem_instance.dataset_name: Sparkov credit card transactions fraud dataset

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic credit-card transaction data generated by Sparkov; feature-engineered to 20 dimensions for the main experiments; evaluation at anomaly ratio r=0.2 uses 500 samples split into 450 train and 50 test.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Subsampled to keep 100 anomalous samples and add normal samples to control anomaly ratio; feature engineering included fraud-rate encodings for categorical variables, binary gender dummies, and dropping unused variables; train-test split 9:1 for the main benchmark.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation for model comparison; repeated over 10 different dataset splits for r=0.2 to estimate probability of outperforming classical baseline; 450/50 train-test split for hardware benchmarks.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Feature engineering on Sparkov data; partial state tomography simulated with equally distributed Pauli measurements; 1Q-RDMs averaged over 200 snapshots per qubit.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: F1 score computed on train and test splits; probability of qrbf outperforming rbf estimated under truncated normal assumption.

speedup_claims.conditions: No asymptotic or computational speedup is claimed; only improved generalization/F1 is reported.
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports better test F1 for qrbf-OCSVM in simulation, but this is not a runtime speedup.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not specified; would require scaling quantum kernel circuits and tomography beyond the 10‑qubit feature map and hundreds of samples used here.
limiting_factors: Kernel estimation requires classical shadow tomography with many measurements per sample
Small dataset (≤10^4 samples in simulation benchmarks)
Only 10 qubits used in feature map
Kernel SVM training still performed classically (LIBSVM)

notes: num_qubits inferred as 10 from Appendix A feature maps showing q0 through q9, i.e. 10 qubits.
hardware.type set to simulator_other because the benchmark in Sec. III.A is explicitly described as simulations with finite-sampling noise, not a real QPU.
Authors report higher F1 scores for qrbf-OCSVM compared to classical rbf-OCSVM in simulation (Fig. 1) but do not demonstrate computational advantage or scaling benefits.

experiments.description: Partial state tomography of single-qubit states on real superconducting hardware to assess tomography precision versus shot count.

algorithm.variant: Partial state tomography / shadow tomography protocol

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Prepare known single-qubit states and reconstruct their density matrices from Pauli-basis measurements.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate density matrix rho_exp and compare to true rho via Frobenius norm distance d(rho,rho_exp).

problem_instance.description: Tomography benchmark on prepared single-qubit states |+> and |T> on IBM Falcon r2.

dataset_specification.description: Single-qubit state-preparation benchmark; no external dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Pauli random measurement basis transformations using H, HS^†, or identity; equal shot allocation across bases.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Each shot count repeated 100 times; compare simulator and hardware tomography precision as a function of shots.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: State preparation and Pauli-basis measurement selection.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Reconstruct density matrices and compute Frobenius norm distance d(rho,rho_exp).

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: precision improves with shots on simulator; saturates on hardware beyond ~10^3 shots

speedup_claims.conditions: The experiment studies tomography precision versus shot count; no speedup claim is made.
speedup_claims.caveats: Hardware precision saturates beyond about 10^3 shots due to calibration drift and SPAM; simulator continues improving polynomially.

limiting_factors: Experiment is purely a tomography precision benchmark
No classical comparison for computational advantage

notes: num_qubits inferred as 1 because the benchmark prepares and tomographs single-qubit states |+> and |T>.
hardware.type reported as IBM Falcon r2 superconducting QPU.
This experiment evaluates tomography precision on hardware and is not intended to demonstrate algorithmic advantage.

experiments.description: Hardware benchmark of the qrbf-OCSVM anomaly detector on real trapped-ion and superconducting quantum processors using three hardware-efficient feature maps.

algorithm.variant: One-Class Quantum Support Vector Machine with projected qrbf kernel on hardware-efficient feature maps
algorithm.optimizer: LIBSVM / quadratic programming solver (for OCSVM dual)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 20-dimensional fraud-detection samples encoded into 10-qubit hardware-efficient circuits; projected kernels computed from 1Q-RDMs obtained by partial tomography.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Same qrbf-OCSVM objective as in simulation: OCSVM dual with projected quantum kernel from 1Q-RDMs.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: OCSVM dual constraints; no QUBO/penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Fraud detection on the feature-engineered Sparkov dataset at anomaly ratio r=0.2.
problem_instance.dataset_name: Sparkov credit card transactions fraud dataset

dataset_specification.description: 500 samples total, split into 450 train and 50 test; anomaly ratio r=0.2; same feature-engineered dataset as simulation benchmark.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Same feature engineering and subsampling as the simulation benchmark; tomography-based kernel estimation on hardware.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: F1 score on train and test split; compared against noise-free simulator and classical rbf-OCSVM; repeated 128 times in simulation to estimate standard deviation in the noise-free regime.

hardware.device_name: AQT Ibex, IonQ Harmony, IBM Brisbane, IBM Sherbrooke, IBM Osaka

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Partial state tomography with Pauli random measurements; 1Q-RDMs used to build projected kernels.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute F1 scores for train/test and compare across hardware and simulator.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: F1 fluctuates around simulator value due to tomography error and hardware noise

speedup_claims.conditions: No runtime speedup is claimed; the comparison is on anomaly-detection performance.
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the qrbf models outperform the classical baseline in F1 on the test data, but also notes that more experimental data is needed to confirm robustness under hardware noise.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require significantly larger qubit counts and faster tomography/kernel estimation to handle large financial datasets.
limiting_factors: Only 10 qubits used in feature map
Dataset extremely small (500 samples with r=0.2)
Kernel estimation requires tomography with 200 shots per qubit per sample
Hybrid pipeline dominated by classical computation
No scaling study demonstrating improved asymptotic complexity

notes: num_qubits inferred as 10 from the feature maps in Appendix A (q0 through q9).
Hardware benchmark includes AQT Ibex, IonQ Harmony, and IBM Eagle/Falcon devices; representative device_name recorded as AQT Ibex and hardware.type as trapped ion for this experiment entry.

Paper claims better generalization (higher F1 scores) than classical rbf‑OCSVM and reports similar performance on real QPUs (Fig. 3), but experiments are small-scale and do not establish computational quantum advantage.
